The excerpts give two different weekly rates, and none of them says which one is current.

- One version of the guidance says you can get up to £123.25 per week Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) if you're too ill to work, paid by your employer for up to 28 weeks [Print Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) - GOV.UK-0001]. In this version, you get £123.25 a week or 80% of your normal weekly earnings, whichever is lower [Print Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) - GOV.UK-0002].
- A version labelled 2025 says you can get £116.75 per week SSP, paid by your employer for up to 28 weeks [Print Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) 2025 - GOV.UK-0001].

Both versions say you cannot get less than the statutory amount, and you may get more if your employer has a company sick pay scheme [Print Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) - GOV.UK-0001] [Print Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) 2025 - GOV.UK-0001].

The version with the £116.75 rate is labelled 2025 and has web-archive links, which suggests it is an older, archived copy. That hints £123.25 is the newer rate, but the excerpts don't state which rate is current, so check the date of each source to confirm.

After the first 6 weeks, Statutory Maternity Pay is paid for the next 33 weeks at a flat weekly rate or 90% of your average weekly earnings, whichever is lower [Print Maternity pay and leave - GOV.UK-0003]. The excerpts give two different figures for that flat rate. One document gives £194.32 a week [Print Maternity pay and leave - GOV.UK-0003]. Another gives £184.03 a week [Print Maternity pay and leave 2025 - GOV.UK-0003].

The documents don't say which rate is current. The £184.03 version links to web-archive copies of GOV.UK pages [Print Maternity pay and leave 2025 - GOV.UK-0003], so it is probably an older snapshot. The worked examples show the same split: one uses £194.32 a week [Print Shared Parental Leave and Pay - GOV.UK-0008] and the other uses £184.03 a week [Print Shared Parental Leave and Pay 2025- GOV.UK-0005]. So £194.32 a week, or 90% of average weekly earnings if that is lower, looks like the more recent rate. The excerpts don't confirm that it is the current one.

Yes. Paternity Leave can be split into two separate one-week blocks. You can take up to 2 weeks' leave, either both weeks together or separately in one-week blocks [Print Paternity pay and leave - GOV.UK-0003]. Under the NHS policy, you can take a single period of one or two weeks, or split it into two periods of one week at different times. The leave has to be taken in complete weeks, not as odd days off [UHN-PO-HR10-0036]. If you take Paternity Leave in two separate one-week blocks, you must claim at least 28 days before the second week [Print Paternity pay and leave - GOV.UK-0012].

As for timing, the leave cannot start before the birth. It must end within 52 weeks of the baby's birth, or within 52 weeks of the due date if the baby is early [Print Paternity pay and leave - GOV.UK-0003]. The NHS policy also says the leave can be taken up to 52 weeks after the birth, or after the placement date in the case of adoption [UHN-PO-HR10-0036].

Older rules applied if the baby was due on or before 6 April 2024. In that case you could take 1 or 2 weeks' leave, but it had to be taken in one go and end within 56 days of the birth, or of the due date if the baby is early [Print Paternity pay and leave 2025- GOV.UK-0004]. If the baby was due after 6 April 2024, the 2 weeks can be taken together or separately, and the leave must end within 52 weeks of the birth [Print Paternity pay and leave 2025- GOV.UK-0004].

To qualify for Statutory Maternity Pay (SMP), you must earn on average at least £123 a week [Print Maternity pay and leave 2025 - GOV.UK-0005]. You must also give the correct notice and proof that you're pregnant. And you must have worked for your employer continuously for at least 26 weeks continuing into the 'qualifying week', which is the 15th week before the expected week of childbirth [Print Maternity pay and leave 2025 - GOV.UK-0005]. If you don't have earnings equal to the lower earnings limit for National Insurance contributions, you won't get statutory maternity pay, but you can apply for Maternity Allowance [UHN-PO-HR10-0022].

The provided documents don't give a minimum average weekly earnings threshold for Statutory Paternity Pay. The paternity excerpts only give the weekly rate: £194.32 in one version [Print Paternity pay and leave - GOV.UK-0006] and £184.03 in the other [Print Paternity pay and leave 2025- GOV.UK-0006]. In both versions, you get that amount or 90% of your average weekly earnings, whichever is lower.

To be eligible for Statutory Shared Parental Pay (ShPP), each parent must earn on average at least £123 a week [Print Shared Parental Leave and Pay 2025- GOV.UK-0002]. If only the mother's partner takes the SPL and ShPP, the partner must earn on average at least £123 a week [Print Shared Parental Leave and Pay 2025- GOV.UK-0002]. If only the mother takes them, the mother must earn on average at least £123 a week [Print Shared Parental Leave and Pay 2025- GOV.UK-0002]. The other parent must instead meet an earnings test of at least £390 in total across any 13 of the 66 weeks before the week the baby is due [Print Shared Parental Leave and Pay 2025- GOV.UK-0002].

Caveat: the £123 figure comes from the 2025 archived version of the guidance. There is a later version of the guidance, and it gives a higher ShPP rate (£194.32 a week, up from £184.03) [Print Shared Parental Leave and Pay - GOV.UK-0009] [Print Maternity pay and leave 2025 - GOV.UK-0003]. However, that later excerpt does not give the minimum earnings figure. So I can't confirm from these documents that £123 is still the current threshold.
